name: Theophylline

lead: Theophylline is a prescription drug related to caffeine, used for asthma and COPD. It was first used medically as a diuretic in 1902.
It appears among de-puffing compounds because of that diuretic history. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or appearance.

paras: It inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors, relaxing airway muscle and affecting the heart and kidneys. It is cleared by liver CYP1A2.

The US label describes a narrow safety margin: nausea, headache and insomnia at lower levels, and arrhythmias, seizures and death at high levels. Many drugs and smoking change its clearance. It is prescription-only.

lead: Theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) is a methylxanthine drug that inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors. It is prescribed for chronic asthma, COPD and apnea of prematurity, and occurs naturally in small amounts in tea [1][2]. Its first clinical use, in 1902, was as a diuretic, before it was adopted for asthma about two decades later [1].

In appearance-related discussion it is listed among de-puffing compounds because of that diuretic history. No published study has tested theophylline for facial puffiness, water retention or other cosmetic outcomes. It has a narrow therapeutic window, and the US label warns that blood levels above 20 mcg/mL can cause persistent vomiting, arrhythmias and seizures that can be lethal [3].

paras: The US label indicates theophylline for symptoms and reversible airflow obstruction in chronic asthma and other chronic lung diseases such as emphysema and chronic bronchitis [3]. Reference sources describe it as largely a second-line agent today, with inhaled therapies preferred [1][2].

Theophylline relaxes airway smooth muscle by inhibiting PDE3 and to a lesser extent PDE4, and antagonises adenosine receptors; it also has anti-inflammatory actions including activation of histone deacetylases [1][3]. It is cleared mainly by CYP1A2, so smoking, liver disease, heart failure and interacting drugs such as erythromycin, cimetidine, fluoroquinolones and fluvoxamine change blood levels [1].

Below peak serum levels of 20 mcg/mL, adverse effects are described as generally mild and caffeine-like: nausea, vomiting, headache and insomnia. Above that level the label lists persistent vomiting, cardiac arrhythmias and seizures that can be lethal, and warns of extreme caution in peptic ulcer, seizure disorders and arrhythmias [3]. Clinicians monitor serum concentrations because of the narrow therapeutic range [1].
Albrecht Kossel extracted it from tea leaves around 1888; Emil Fischer and Lorenz Ach published a synthesis in 1895, and Wilhelm Traube introduced another method in 1900 [1][2].

Registered trials of theophylline address respiratory and other medical conditions, including bronchiectasis [4], COPD exacerbations [5], syncope linked to low adenosine [6], diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill patients [7], and pseudohypoparathyroidism [8]. No study found examined theophylline for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes.
